title: Bibliotheken en scholen kunnen bordspel CODER.IO aanvragen voor programmeren zonder scherm
raw_text: Bibliotheken die met scholen samenwerken, schoolbibliotheken en mediatheken kunnen tot en met 30 november kosteloos het bordspel CODER.IO aanvragen. Met het spel leren leerlingen vanaf 10 jaar programmeren zonder scherm. OCLC geeft twaalf exemplaren cadeau aan de Bibliotheek op school, ter ere van twee jubilea: Jeugdbieb.nl bestaat 25 jaar en productanalist Marcel Wijngaard werkt dit jaar 25 jaar bij OCLC. Zijn kinderen bedachten het spel. Wijngaards zoon Edwin programmeert al sinds zijn zesde. Toen hij als tienjarige minder op zijn scherm mocht, ging hij aan de keukentafel verder met post-its, getekende kaartjes en zelfgemaakte poppetjes. Samen met zijn zus Anna werkte hij het idee in tweeënhalf jaar uit tot een bordspel. In 2025 brachten ze het uit bij hun eigen uitgeverij Vinea Games. Hoe CODER.IO werkt In CODER.IO zijn spelers een robot die via een portaal terug naar huis wil. De route leggen ze met codekaarten, zoals vooruit, draaien en springen. Loopt de robot vast, dan zoeken de spelers de fout en verbeteren ze hun code. In latere levels komen herhalingen en als-dan-opdrachten erbij. Digitale geletterdheid Digitale geletterdheid krijgt een vaste plek in het onderwijs. De Eerste Kamer stemde in juni in met de wet en de nieuwe kerndoelen digitale geletterdheid gelden naar verwachting vanaf 1 augustus 2027. title: Statement from the IFLA Governing Board on SIGL and communications from IFLA Members
raw_text: The IFLA Governing Board notes the recent correspondence on IFLA-L concerning SIGL and regrets that matters have reached this point. At the same time, we recognise the concerns raised by members, particularly regarding the level of expenditure incurred by SIGL, given its current governance structure of three Board members and one adviser. IFLA has separately been undertaking its own due diligence in relation to these matters. In the interests of transparency, we would welcome SIGL making its full audit report for 2025 available. We would also welcome greater clarity regarding the role of its adviser, Mr Gerald Leitner, including the scope of the role, remuneration and contractual terms. We also regret that SIGL did not take forward the suggestion that former IFLA President Vicki McDonald join its Board. We believe that such an appointment would have provided an important and constructive demonstration of openness and transparency, as well as helping to rebuild confidence. Our overriding priority is to ensure that the Legacy Grant is used for its intended purpose: to strengthen the global library field . We remain committed to ensuring that concerns about its governance and use are addressed transparently, factually and in the interests of IFLA and its members. raw_text: Roel Zuidhof wordt per 1 maart 2027 de nieuwe directeur-bestuurder van FlevoMeer Bibliotheek. Daarmee komt een einde aan de periode van interim-bestuur. Zuidhof gaat leidinggeven aan de bibliotheekorganisatie die actief is in de gemeenten Dronten, Lelystad, Noordoostpolder, Urk en Zeewolde. Zuidhof verlaat Bibliotheek Nieuwegein waar hij ook directeur-bestuurder was. Roel Zuidhof heeft ruime ervaring in de bibliotheeksector. Gedurende zijn loopbaan werkte hij in de bibliotheeksector, waaronder bij Bibliotheek Nijkerk en andere bibliotheekorganisaties. De afgelopen vijf jaar was Roel directeur-bestuurder van Bibliotheek Nieuwegein. Hij brengt daarmee brede kennis en ervaring mee van de ontwikkelingen en uitdagingen binnen de bibliotheeksector. Zuidhof ziet een belangrijke maatschappelijke rol voor de bibliotheek. title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
raw_text: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
raw_text: Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...] If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

title: llm-anthropic 0.31
raw_text: Release: llm-anthropic 0.31 Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. Fable 5.2 is currently ranked first on Artificial Analysis . Anthropic say it "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes", so clearly their internal benchmarks have become more ambitious! I've added the new models to llm-anthropic , so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this: uv tool install llm llm install llm-anthropic llm keys set anthropic # paste key here llm -m claude-fable-5.2 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh : max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them . That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine. It's priced at $8/million input and $40/million output, which is a 20% discount on the previous Fable 5.1 ($10/$50). I also used Fable 5.2 to help identify the source of a mysterious beep . title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
raw_text: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. raw_text: From a Google Research Blog Post: Building products that reflect the world’s linguistic diversity takes far more than software engineering; it requires close collaboration with the communities we aim to serve, building in a way that’s deeply aligned and respectful of local communities, heritage, history, values and context. [Clip] But gathering this data is only one part of the journey. Preserving language vitality requires working closely with native speakers, academic institutions, and cultural organizations. Partnerships, such as our coalition with the Gates Foundation , ensure that modern digital tools reflect the nuances and authentic voices of their communities. Expanding language coverage responsibly also requires deeply understanding linguistic diversity on a global scale. This approach enables products like Gboard , our Android keyboard, to support 900+ language varieties. To better appreciate the breadth and complexity of this speech diversity, we’ve been working on a tool to help visualize the world’s linguistic diversity, inspired by earlier visualization initiatives like Google Earth . The Language Explorer is an interactive web platform designed to let researchers, educators, and language enthusiasts discover and visualize linguistic diversity around the world. Developed as part of our 1,000 Languages Initiative , the Language Explorer brings together data across thousands of languages, building on our open-source LinguaMeta dataset . title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
raw_text: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
raw_text: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
raw_text: Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting. Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones. Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. title: Review: Apple's M6 MacBook Pro is good, but it's missing all the exciting stuff
raw_text: I've written more than once about the weird positioning of Apple's entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro, which has always occupied an uncomfortable perch between the MacBook Air and the higher-end MacBook Pros. The best versions of this laptop, like last year's M5 refresh, come with the same basic design and external features of the higher-end MacBook Pros, just with a more modest processor and a lower ceiling for specs like RAM and storage. The lesser versions stick with older designs or other compromises, reserving Apple's most updated designs and screen technologies for the more expensive high-end models. Recall the 13-inch M1 and M2 MacBook Pros, which stuck with Apple's 2016-era MacBook Pro designs for everything , up to and including the now-abandoned Touch Bar. (If you're someone at Apple maintaining Touch Bar support into the 2030s for the sake of these two laptop models, I'd like to hear from you. Not for a story! I'd just like to know how you are.) This year's entry-level MacBook Pro mostly falls into that latter category. It does get an Apple M6 chip, and the M6 is great—rumors suggest the M6 won't get Pro, Max, or Ultra configurations, so there are some fringe benefits here that you can't get in the top-tier MacBook Pros. But it uses the same MacBook Pro design Apple has been using since 2021 . There's no touchscreen, no OLED panel, no Dynamic Island, no half-pound weight reduction, no glowing Apple logo on the lid.
